desc:
A startup has w units of capital and may complete at most k projects, one after another. Project i can be started only if the current capital is at least capital[i] (the amount is a requirement, it is not spent), and when it is finished the capital grows by profits[i]. Each project can be done once.

Return the largest capital you can hold after finishing at most k projects.

k = 2, w = 0, profits = [1, 2, 3], capital = [0, 1, 1] -> 4
k = 3, w = 0, profits = [1, 2, 3], capital = [0, 1, 2] -> 6
k = 1, w = 5, profits = [4, 9], capital = [6, 5]        -> 14

In the first example start with project 0 (capital becomes 1), then take project 2 with profit 3 (capital 4).
hints: Profits are never negative, so more capital never hurts. At each step, among the projects you can currently afford, which one should you do?
The one with the largest profit: it raises your capital the most and also unlocks the most new projects. The difficulty is knowing which projects are affordable as capital grows.

Sort projects by required capital. Keep a max-heap of profits of the affordable projects: before each of the k rounds move every project with capital ≤ w into the heap, then pop the largest profit and add it to w. Stop early if the heap is empty.
editorial: Because profits are non-negative and the requirement is not consumed, capital is monotone: doing a project can only make more projects available. In each of the k rounds the best move is to complete the affordable project with the largest profit. An exchange argument shows it: any plan that picks a smaller affordable profit now can swap it for the larger one, ending with at least the same capital and a superset of unlocked projects.

To find that project quickly, sort the projects by required capital. Keep a pointer into the sorted list and a max-heap of profits. In each round, move all projects with capital ≤ w from the sorted list into the heap, then pop the largest profit and add it to w. If the heap is empty, no project is affordable and we stop.
Sorting is O(n log n), and every project enters and leaves the heap at most once, so the total is O((n + k) log n).
solution:
import heapq


def finalCapital(k, w, profits, capital):
    projects = sorted(zip(capital, profits))
    heap = []
    i = 0
    n = len(projects)
    for _ in range(k):
        while i < n and projects[i][0] <= w:
            heapq.heappush(heap, -projects[i][1])
            i += 1
        if not heap:
            break
        w -= heapq.heappop(heap)
    return w
